 Judgment

The legal heir of the plaintiff, being aggrieved by the concurrent findings of the Munsiff's Court,
Perintalmanna, in O.S.No.96/1983, as affirmed by the Sub Court, Manjeri, in A.S.No.19/2011, has come up in the present appeal.

2. The brief facts necessary for the disposal of the appeal are as follows:
2.1.
The suit was filed initially for a mandatory injunction requiring the original defendant to vacate the property on termination of the tenancy.

Initially, the suit was dismissed by judgment dated 29.02.1992 and aggrieved, the plaintiff preferred an appeal before the District Court, Manjeri, as A.S.No.131/1992, which was allowed by judgment dated 12.04.2002 by accepting the prayer for amendment of the plaint and converting the same for recovery of possession and accordingly setting aside the findings of the Trial Court
, the suit was restored.
Thereafter, the suit was tried afresh.

2.2. The plaint schedule property having a building was let out 2025:KER:73853 to the original defendant on 24.12.1962 for a rent of Rs.5/- per month and later on 24.01.1980, the rent was enhanced to Rs.15/- per month.
The defendant paid the rent up to August 1980.

Thereafter, since there was a default in the payment of the rent,
on 17.06.1983 a notice was issued to the original defendant demanding vacant possession and terminating the tenancy with effect from 25.7.1983.

2.3. The defendant contested the suit by denying the existence of the tenancy and that according to the defendant, the property was entrusted by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff under an oral entrustment for permanent enjoyment of the building.
Later, the original defendant constructed a small shed, wherein he started a tea shop and later constructed a building and he continued the tea shop there.
The extent of the property is 6 1/2 x 4 1/2 six feet koles.
It was given as 'SASWATHAVAKASAM' for enjoyment without any liability.

The plaintiff tried to obtain purchase certificate in respect of the plaint schedule property, which was not issued by the Land Tribunal and therefore, the findings of the Land Tribunal on the question of the title of the plaintiff have become final and therefore, the same cannot be reagitated.
2.4.

Before the Trial Court, on behalf of the plaintiff, Exts.A1 to A6 documents were produced and PW1 was examined and on behalf 2025:KER:73853 of the defendant(s), Exts.B1 series and B2 were marked and DW1 and DW2 were examined.

Before the remand, the Trial Court had framed the following issues:
1.
Whether the plaintiff has right or title over the suit property?

3 2. Whether the entrustment alleged in para 2 of the plaint is true?
3. Whether the defendant is a tenant entitled to fixity of tenure?
4. Whether the defendant has constructed the shop building ?
5. What is the correct extent of the suit property?
6. Whether any damage is caused to the shop building ?
7. Whether the suit is liable to be stayed u/s 125(3) of the K.L.R. Act?
8. What order as to cost and relief?

After remand, the following additional issues were framed:
9: Whether plaintiff is entitled to recover plaint schedule property on the strength of title?
10.Whether there is tenancy in favour of defendatns in respect of plaint schedule property ?
11.Whether
plaintiff
is entitled for compensation for use and occupation

The Trial Court concluded that the right of the plaintiff was extinguished by operation of Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and that the plaintiff cannot maintain a suit for recovery of possession against the defendant because the defendant had perfected title by adverse possession.

Aggrieved, the plaintiff preferred A.S.No.19/2011 before the Sub Court, Manjeri, which was also dismissed, and hence,
the present second appeal.

3. Heard, Sri.Thareeq Anver K.- learned counsel appearing for the appellant/plaintiff and Sri.R.Rajesh Kormath - learned counsel 2025:KER:73853 appearing for the respondents/defendants.
4.
Sri.Thareeq Anver K. - learned counsel appearing for the appellant/plaintiff contended that the finding of the courts below that the suit was barred by limitation is erroneous.

It is the specific case of the learned counsel that the occupation of the defendants, if any, can only be construed as one permissive and once it is concluded that the occupation is permissive, then the plea of perfection of title by adverse possession cannot be sustained.

Referring to Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963,
the learned counsel for the appellant further submitted that the appellant needs to institute the suit within 12 years from the date on which the tenancy was terminated or a demand for vacant possession was made by the plaintiff.

This was in the year Raveendran vs Sarojini (Died) on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190122606/
4 1983, when Ext.A4 notice was issued and the suit having been instituted in the year 1983 itself, no case of adverse possession is made out, and that the courts below misconstrued the principles underlying the application of Section 27 and Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963.

In support of his contention, he relied on the decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rabindranath Panigrahi v. Surendra Sahu [2025 INSC 333] and Ram Nagina Rai and Another v. Deo Kumar Rai (Deceased) by Lrs &
Another [(2019) 13 SCC 324].

6. In reply, the learned counsel for the appellant - Sri.Thareeq Anver K., by placing reliance on the decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Thakur Kishan Singh (Dead) v. Arvind Kumar [AIR 1995 SC 73] pointed out that, when the defendant claimed to have started occupation of the building based on a permission, it must be construed as one granted under a licence and therefore, on termination of the licence, he will have to hand over vacant possession of the property.

7. I have considered the rival submissions raised across the Bar and have perused the judgments of the courts below and the records of the case.

8. While admitting the appeal, this Court framed the following substantial question of law:
"Are the courts below justified in non-suiting the plaintiff finding that the defendants have perfected title by adverse possession, when the defendants themselves set up a lease?"

5 9.
The issue raised in the appeal falls on a narrow compass.
The possession of the defendants over the plaint schedule building is 2025:KER:73853 indisputable.

It is also a common case that the predecessor-in- interest of the plaintiff entrusted the plaint schedule building to the original defendant, but the dispute is only in the manner of such entrustment.

The plaintiff claims that it is under a tenancy agreement that the building was entrusted to the defendant, whereas the defendants would contend that the building was entrusted by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff by an oral entrustment, what is called as 'SASWATHAVAKASAM'.

Before going into the question as to whether the right of the plaintiff stood extinguished by operation of Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963, one needs to properly decipher the nature of possession of the defendant.

10. The law regarding adverse possession needs no further exploration at the hands of this Court,
especially since the law is well settled.
Adverse possession arises when the defendant's possession is hostile to the plaintiff, with full and open knowledge of the plaintiff that the property being possessed belongs to the plaintiff.
Therefore, in legal parlance, the possession of the defendants should be with animus possidendi.
In a plea of adverse possession, it is trite law that the title of the plaintiff has to be admitted.

But when the defendants sets up the plea of adverse possession by tracing their title through any separate means, then, the plea of adverse possession and the claim of independent right will not go together.

In the present case, what is pleaded in the written statement and argued before this Court is that the original defendant came into possession of the plaint schedule property from the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff through an oral entrustment or 'SASWATHAVAKASAM'.
It is an admitted case that there is no document of conveyance.
In terms of Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, any conveyance which intends to transfer right over a property having a value of more than Rs.100/-, requires registration.
Admittedly, no registered document is executed by the predecessor- in-interest of the plaintiff in favour of the original defendant.
Therefore, it is irresistible for this Court to conclude that, what is claimed by the defendants is nothing but an oral entrustment.
The oral entrustment can at the best be construed as one granting permission to the defendants to occupy the premises.
A right to use a particular building or a land granted by the plaintiff to the defendants cannot crystalize into a claim of perfection of title by adverse possession.

12. In Pt.Shamboo Nath Tikoo and Others v. S.Gian Singh and Others [1995 Supp (3) SCC 266], the Supreme Court considered the question as to whether a permissive occupant could claim adverse possession.

13. In L.N. Aswathama and Another v. P. Prakash [(2009) 13 SCC 229], the Hon'ble Supreme Court carved out the basic requirement to sustain the plea of adverse possession.

Paragraph 17 of the judgment reads as under:
"17.
The legal position is no doubt well settled.

To establish a claim of title by prescription, that is, adverse possession for 12 years or more, the possession of the Raveendran vs Sarojini (Died) on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190122606/
6 claimant must be physical/actual, exclusive, open, uninterrupted, notorious and hostile to the true owner for a period exceeding twelve years.
It is also well settled that long and continuous possession by itself would not constitute adverse possession if it was either permissive possession or possession without animus possidendi.
The pleas based on title and adverse possession are mutually inconsistent and the latter does not begin to operate until the former is renounced.

Unless the person possessing the property has the requisite animus to possess the property hostile to the title of the true owner, the period for prescription will not commence.(Vide:
Periasami vs. P. Periathambi [1995 (6) SCC 523], Md. Mohammad Ali (dead) by Lrs.
vs. Jagdish Kalita [2004 (1) SCC 271] and P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy vs. Revamma [2007 (6) SCC 59])."
14.

15. In Rabindranath Panigrahi v. Surendra Sahu [2025 INSC 333], the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that when the relationship between the plaintiff - defendant is that of a landlord and tenant, the tenant cannot set up a claim for adverse possession against the landlord.

sentences.text: 16. In the light of the principles carved out by the Hon'ble Supreme Court as above, this Court proceeds to consider the contention raised by the respondents in support of their plea that the right of the plaintiff is lost by adverse possession.

The learned counsel for the respondents - Sri.R.Rajesh Kormath, placed extensive reliance on the decision of the Allahabad High Court in Bharit and Others v The Hon'ble Board of Revenue, U.P. at Allahabad and others [AIR 1973 All 201], which followed the decision of the Supreme Court in Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Bombay and Others [AIR (38) 1951 SC 469], to contend that even if the grant in favour of the defendants is invalid, the defendants are entitled to protect its possession based on Article 65 of the Limitation Act read with Section 27.

The decisions cited across the Bar by the learned counsel for the respondents, rendered 2025:KER:73853 by the various other High Courts on the same point,
also support its plea as aforesaid.

But the pertinent question is whether the ratio decidendi laid down by the High Court of Allahabad and other High Courts in the decisions cited across the Bar would aid the case of the respondents/defendants.

17. In Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Bombay and Others [AIR (38)
1951 SC 469], the Supreme Court considered the plea of a person in possession of a property based on an invalid grant and held that a person who is put in possession of the property on the basis of an invalid grant is entitled to claim possession being adverse to the plaintiff.

sentences.text: "What, in the circumstances was the legal position of the respondent Corporation and its predecessor in title in relation to the land in question?
They were in possession of the land to which they had no legal title at all.

Therefore, the position of the respondent Corporation and its predecessor in title was that of a person having no legal title but nevertheless holding possession of the land under colour of an invalid grant of the land in perpetuity and free from rent for the purpose of a market.

Such possession not being referable to any legal title it was prima facie adverse to the legal title of the Government as owner of the land from the very moment the predecessor in title of the respondent corporation took possession of the land under the invalid grant.

This possession has continued openly as of right and uninterruptedly for over 70 years and the respondent Corporation has acquired the limited title it and its predecessor in title had been prescribing for during all this period, that is to say, the right to hold the land in perpetuity, free from rent but only for the purpose of a market in terms of the Government Resolution of 1865.

The immunity from the liability to pay rent is just as much an integral part or an inseverable incident of the title so acquired 2025:KER:73853 as is the obligation to hold the land for the purpose of a market and for no other purpose.
There is no question of acquisition by adverse possession of the Government's prerogative right to levy assessment.

What the respondent corporation has acquired is the legal right to hold the land in perpetuity free of rent for the specific purpose of erecting and maintaining a market upon the terms of the Government Resolution as if a legal grant had been made to it.

The right thus acquired includes, as part of it, an immunity from payment of rent which must necessarily constitute a right in limitation of the Government's right to assess in excess of the specific limit established and preserved by the Government Resolution within the meaning of S. 8 of the Bombay Act II [2] of 1876."

18. In State of West Bengal v. The Dalhousie Institute Society [AIR 1970 SC 1778], the Supreme Court held that, even if there is nothing to show that the grant has been made in the manner required by law, even then the possession based on the grant can crystalize into a claim of adverse possession.

"16. There is no material placed before us to show that the grant has been made in the manner required by law though as a fact a grant of the site has been made in favour of the Institute.

The evidence relied on by the Special Land Acquisition Judge and the High Court also clearly establishes that the respondent has been in open, continuous and uninterrupted possession and enjoyment of the site for over 60 years.

In this respect the material documentary evidence referred to by the High Court clearly establishes that the respondent has been treated as owner of the site not only by the Corporation, but also by the Government.
The possession of the respondent must have been on the basis of the grant made by the Government, which, no doubt, is invalid in law.

As to what exactly is the legal effect of such possession has been considered by this Court in Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corpn. of the City of Bombay, 1952 SCR 43 (AIR 1951 SC 469) as follows:

This possession has continued openly,
as of right and uninterruptedly for over 70 years and the respondent Corporation has acquired the limited title to it and its predecessor in title had been prescribing for during all this period, that is to say, the right to hold the land in perpetuity free from rent but only for the purposes of a market in terms of the Government Resolution of 1865..."
17. The above extract establishes that a person in such possession clearly acquires title by adverse possession.
In the case before us there are concurrent findings recorded by the High Court and the Special Land Acquisition Judge in favour of the respondent on this point and we agree with those findings."
19. The question before this Court is whether the grant in favour of the original defendant can be construed as an invalid grant or a mere permissive possession.
Admittedly, no documents are produced by the defendants to evidence the so called 'SASWATHAVAKASAM' claimed by them.

Therefore, this Court must necessarily conclude that the possession of the defendants is nothing but a permissive grant through an oral entrustment of the property by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff.

It must be remembered that, it is only in the reply notice and the written statement filed in the suit that the defendants set up a case of 'SASWATHAVAKASAM', which is unfortunately not supported by any evidence.

Therefore, when the facts pleaded before the Court disclose that when both parties claim entrustment and that the dispute is only as regards the manner of 2025:KER:73853 entrustment, it is for the defendants to show that what is claimed is not a permissive possession, but an entitlement to enjoy the property permanently, which then would lead to an invalid grant in the absence of any registered document.
It must be remembered that, the law does not permit a person to claim permanent right over a land and building unless it is accompanied by a registered document.

The precedents cited across the bar by the learned Counsel for the respondents do not speak for a proposition that, a defendant who came into possession based on a permission can be permitted to set up a claim of adverse possession.

Therefore, with the materials on record, this Court is not persuaded to hold that, the defendants came into possession of the plaint schedule property through an invalid grant but on contrary such possession can only be construed as permissive.

20. Alternatively, it is contended by the learned counsel for the respondents that, in the light of the findings of the Land Tribunal in O.A.87/1973 dated 26.05.1997, the title of the plaintiff cannot be reagitated.
The Land Tribunal found that the plaintiff has no title over the property in question and therefore, the courts below were justified in declining the prayer for recovery of possession.
This Court is afraid that the aforesaid contention is completely misplaced.

A perusal of Ext.B2 order shows that, the application for assignment of 2025:KER:73853 right over the property was Raveendran vs Sarojini (Died) on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190122606/
9 dismissed for fault, since the application was not accompanied by sufficient documentary evidence.
Liberty was granted to the plaintiff to file appropriate application for assignment after production of the necessary documents.
Therefore, the contention as regards the loss of title of the plaintiff
cannot be appreciated and is only liable to be rejected.

As an upshot of these discussions, this Court is persuaded to hold that the concurrent findings of the courts below are vitiated by perverse appreciation of the law and facts resulting in miscarriage of justice in favour of the plaintiff.
Resultantly, the substantial question of law framed in the regular second appeal is answered in favour of the appellant/plaintiff.
It is held that the claim of the plaintiff is not barred by adverse possession.

Accordingly, the judgment and decree dated 19.10.2012 in A.S.No.19/2011 on the files of Sub Court, Manjeri, and that of the Munsiff's Court, Perintalmanna dated 30.08.2003 in O.S.No.96/1983 are set aside.
Consequently, O.S.No.96/1983 will stand decreed as prayed for.
The appellant/plaintiff will be entitled to costs throughout.

opennyai_summary.facts:
The suit was filed initially for a mandatory injunction requiring the original defendant to vacate the property on termination of the tenancy.
The defendant paid the rent up to August 1980.
2.3. The defendant contested the suit by denying the existence of the tenancy and that according to the defendant, the property was entrusted by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff under an oral entrustment for permanent enjoyment of the building.
The plaintiff tried to obtain purchase certificate in respect of the plaint schedule property, which was not issued by the Land Tribunal and therefore, the findings of the Land Tribunal on the question of the title of the plaintiff have become final and therefore, the same cannot be reagitated.
2.4.
The Trial Court concluded that the right of the plaintiff was extinguished by operation of Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and that the plaintiff cannot maintain a suit for recovery of possession against the defendant because the defendant had perfected title by adverse possession.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
In support of his contention, he relied on the decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rabindranath Panigrahi v. Surendra Sahu [2025 INSC 333] and Ram Nagina Rai and Another v. Deo Kumar Rai (Deceased) by Lrs &
Another [(2019) 13 SCC 324].
In support of his contention, he relied on the following decisions: State of West Bengal v. The Dalhousie Institute Society [AIR 1970 SUPREME COURT 1778], Collector of Bombay v. Thoreppa [AIR 1982 KARNATAKA 248], Angara Bhoiani and Others v. Kanhei Misra and Another [AIR 1981 ORISSA 93] and Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul [AIR 1966 SC 735].
The learned counsel for the respondents - Sri.R.Rajesh Kormath, placed extensive reliance on the decision of the Allahabad High Court in Bharit and Others v The Hon'ble Board of Revenue, U.P. at Allahabad and others [AIR 1973 All 201], which followed the decision of the Supreme Court in Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Bombay and Others [AIR (38) 1951 SC 469], to contend that even if the grant in favour of the defendants is invalid, the defendants are entitled to protect its possession based on Article 65 of the Limitation Act read with Section 27.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Adverse possession arises when the defendant's possession is hostile to the plaintiff, with full and open knowledge of the plaintiff that the property being possessed belongs to the plaintiff.
Therefore, in legal parlance, the possession of the defendants should be with animus possidendi.
In a plea of adverse possession, it is trite law that the title of the plaintiff has to be admitted.
But when the defendants sets up the plea of adverse possession by tracing their title through any separate means, then, the plea of adverse possession and the claim of independent right will not go together.
Therefore, it is irresistible for this Court to conclude that, what is claimed by the defendants is nothing but an oral entrustment.
The oral entrustment can at the best be construed as one granting permission to the defendants to occupy the premises.
A right to use a particular building or a land granted by the plaintiff to the defendants cannot crystalize into a claim of perfection of title by adverse possession.
12. In Pt.Shamboo Nath Tikoo and Others v. S.Gian Singh and Others [1995 Supp (3) SCC 266], the Supreme Court considered the question as to whether a permissive occupant could claim adverse possession.
The possession of the respondent must have been on the basis of the grant made by the Government, which, no doubt, is invalid in law.
Therefore, this Court must necessarily conclude that the possession of the defendants is nothing but a permissive grant through an oral entrustment of the property by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff.
Therefore, when the facts pleaded before the Court disclose that when both parties claim entrustment and that the dispute is only as regards the manner of 2025:KER:73853 entrustment, it is for the defendants to show that what is claimed is not a permissive possession, but an entitlement to enjoy the property permanently, which then would lead to an invalid grant in the absence of any registered document.
It must be remembered that, the law does not permit a person to claim permanent right over a land and building unless it is accompanied by a registered document.
Therefore, with the materials on record, this Court is not persuaded to hold that, the defendants came into possession of the plaint schedule property through an invalid grant but on contrary such possession can only be construed as permissive.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Resultantly, the substantial question of law framed in the regular second appeal is answered in favour of the appellant/plaintiff.
It is held that the claim of the plaintiff is not barred by adverse possession.
Accordingly, the judgment and decree dated 19.10.2012 in A.S.No.19/2011 on the files of Sub Court, Manjeri, and that of the Munsiff's Court, Perintalmanna dated 30.08.2003 in O.S.No.96/1983 are set aside.
Consequently, O.S.No.96/1983 will stand decreed as prayed for.
The appellant/plaintiff will be entitled to costs throughout.
